title: Animation Systems - Vertices, Cages, Rigs, Deformation, and Motion
abstract: Connect geometric deformation to character playback, blending, skeletal evaluation, interpolation, state machines, compression, and data-driven motion.
image: /content/blog/Animation Systems - Vertices, Cages, Rigs, Deformation, and Motion/animation-systems.svg
imageAlt: One character mesh progresses from vertex samples and a control cage through a skeleton, muscles, hair strands, facial shapes, and a motion trajectory
lede: Character animation needs both a shape representation and a way to produce motion over time. Vertex, cage, and rig methods define deformation; playback and state logic select motion; blending, FK/IK, skinning, and correctives produce the visible result. Compression changes how motion is stored, while learned methods can supply poses or control policies.

sections.heading: Vertex-based animation: move the final samples
paragraphs: Vertex animation plays a sequence of deformed meshes by updating their vertex positions. It can reproduce motion that is difficult to express with a skeleton, but interpolation requires a consistent correspondence between vertices.
The main storage choices are an explicit geometry cache and texture-based playback. Both preserve sampled motion at the cost of data size and reduced editing freedom.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Choose the storage format according to topology and playback cost.

details.explanation: Stores sampled geometry over time. Point caches usually keep only positions with fixed vertex ordering; broader mesh caches may also store normals and changing connectivity. Quantization or prediction can reduce storage.
Encodes sampled positions or offsets in textures for vertex-shader or compute playback on the GPU. Texture packing changes the storage and access pattern; compression is a separate encoding choice.

aiResearch.summary: AnimateAnyMesh generates mesh motion from text, 4Deform reconstructs intermediate surfaces from sparse observations, and V2M4 turns video into a mesh animation asset. Their outputs reach vertex playback through different representations.

explanations.title: AnimateAnyMesh: generate vertex trajectories
text: A static mesh and action text condition the model. DyMeshVAE separates shape and motion features while retaining local topology; Rectified Flow generates motion in the compressed representation.
The decoder reconstructs per-vertex trajectories on the input mesh. Unlike a rig, this gives direct surface motion rather than editable joint controls.

explanations.title: 4Deform: reconstruct a continuous moving surface
text: Sparse point clouds and limited noisy correspondences constrain a time-varying implicit surface and continuous velocity field. Geometric and physical losses regularize motion between observations.
Querying intermediate times produces reconstructed surfaces. Extracted meshes need not retain the same vertex count or topology, so fixed-topology playback requires a separate correspondence step.

explanations.title: V2M4: turn per-frame reconstruction into a usable asset
text: The method starts from monocular video and generated per-frame meshes, then aligns poses and refines appearance. Pairwise registration addresses inconsistent topology by deforming corresponding geometry through time.
A shared texture and mesh keyframes produce a playable animation asset. Topology alignment belongs to the registration stage; it is not guaranteed by independent frame generation.

sections.heading: Cage-based animation: deform through coordinates
paragraphs: A control cage encloses a detailed mesh with a small number of vertices. Precomputed coordinate weights transfer edits of this coarse boundary to the embedded mesh; the coordinate family determines locality, smoothness, and shape preservation.
The methods below compare how those weights are constructed. Free-Form Deformation uses a parametric lattice instead of the same polygonal-cage formulation.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Coordinate methods trade direct evaluation against locality and directional detail.

details.explanation: Computes smooth generalized barycentric weights directly from cage geometry. The displayed closed-form formula is for a 2D polygon; the 3D extension uses triangular cage faces.

note: x is the query point and v_i is a polygon vertex.
α_{i-1} and α_i are the adjacent angles seen from x around v_i.
w_i is the raw geometric weight; normalization gives φ_i.

details.explanation: Solves a Laplace problem for each handle influence inside the cage. Boundary values govern how influence propagates, allowing localized control in concave cages at a higher precomputation cost.

note: φ_j is handle j’s influence field; prescribed cage-boundary values determine the interior solution.

details.explanation: Uses cage-vertex positions and face normals, adding directional information that helps preserve local detail during rotation and bending.

equation.expression: η′ = F(η; P′) = Σ_{i∈I_V} φ_i(η) v′_i + Σ_{j∈I_T} ψ_j(η) s_j n(t′_j)
note: η and η′ are the original and deformed point; P′ is the edited cage.
φ_i and ψ_j are precomputed vertex and face weights.
The first sum blends edited vertices v′_i; the second blends face normals n(t′_j) with scale factors s_j.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: The control structure also affects the edits a deformation can express.

details.explanation: Builds a coarse enclosure suitable for deformation. Enclosure quality and control placement matter as much as reducing the vertex count.
Embeds geometry in a parametric lattice. Moving its control points bends, twists, or tapers the embedded shape through the lattice basis functions.

aiResearch.summary: These two geometry-processing studies extend cage expressiveness with curved boundaries and polynomial deformation modes. They are analytic deformation methods rather than learned models.

explanations.title: Flexible 3D Cage-based Deformation: replace flat faces with Bézier patches
text: The input is a detailed mesh enclosed by a curved cage made from Bézier patches. The method derives Green coordinates from the positions and normals of the Bézier control net, so a small number of controls can represent smooth, high-curvature boundaries more precisely than a triangle or ruled-quad cage.

Because the coordinates are approximated with Riemann sums, a global projection step restores linear reproduction. The result remains a deterministic cage deformer: no network is trained and the output is still driven by edited cage controls.

explanations.title: Polynomial 3D Green Coordinates: give linear cages curved deformation modes
text: The method starts with a conventional linear triangular cage but derives closed-form polynomial Green coordinates and their derivatives. During deformation, a cage face can map to a polynomial surface, giving artists curved behavior without replacing the asset with a dense control mesh.

The coordinate derivatives also define a smooth subspace for variational shape optimization. This is non-neural companion research: it improves the analytic control representation that an AI-authored or manually authored deformation can use.

equations.expression: x = Σ_j φ_j(x) c_j,   Σ_j φ_j(x)=1
terms: x is the embedded point; c_j are cage vertices and φ_j are their coordinate weights.
Weights sum to one and remain fixed while the controls move.

sections.heading: Rig-based animation: hierarchy, skinning, IK, and retargeting
paragraphs: A rig separates pose control from surface deformation. Controllers specify goals; solvers find joint configurations under constraints; skinning transfers the resulting bone motion to vertices. Local joint transforms compose along the parent hierarchy to give global transforms.

Automatic rigging builds the skeleton, automatic skinning assigns vertex influences, and retargeting transfers existing motion to another character. These are different authoring stages even when one system provides all three.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Controls specify intent; IK methods differ in how they satisfy it.

details.explanation: FK evaluates a pose from local joint transforms. With column vectors, G_j = G_parent L_j: each bone inherits its parent’s component-space transform. Row-vector conventions reverse the written product. IK instead sets an end-effector target and adjusts the intervening joints; both operate on the same hierarchy.
A hand or foot target does not uniquely determine elbow or knee direction. A pole target resolves that bend-plane ambiguity; joint limits and preferred angles further constrain the solution.
Linearizes the relationship between joint changes and end-effector motion, then solves for an update. Useful for redundant chains, but damping is often needed near singular configurations.

note: J maps joint updates Δθ to end-effector changes; J⁺ is its pseudoinverse.
The position difference is the target error. Damped least squares stabilizes near-singular updates.

details.explanation: For a root–joint–end chain, use the two segment lengths and root-to-target distance to solve the middle angle analytically. A pole target supplies the bend plane. Clamp unreachable targets or explicitly permit stretching, and handle fully straight or folded singular configurations.

note: a and b are bone lengths, d is root-to-target distance, and θ is the middle joint’s interior angle.
Clamp the target to |a-b|≤d≤a+b, or explicitly allow stretching.

details.explanation: Cyclic Coordinate Descent usually starts at the end effector’s parent, rotates that joint to reduce end-point error, and moves toward the root. Repeated passes stop at a tolerance or iteration budget. Joint limits and update order affect convergence. This CCD is an IK method, not continuous collision detection.

FABRIK pins the end point to the target and repositions joints back toward the root at fixed segment lengths. It then restores the root anchor and rebuilds the chain outward. Repeat as needed, convert segment directions back into joint rotations, and enforce limits separately.

Coordinates several end-effectors and connected chains, balancing target errors against stiffness, preferred angles, joint limits, and root movement. It describes a solver scope rather than one universal algorithm.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Skinning evaluates the pose relative to the bind configuration.

details.explanation: The skinning matrix is the current bone transform composed with its inverse bind transform. Both must use compatible frames: G_j B_j⁻¹ assumes a common reference frame for mesh and bones. World-space bone transforms need an additional inverse current mesh transform when the output vertex is required in mesh-local space.

LBS transforms a bind-pose vertex with each influencing skinning matrix, then sums the results using normalized skin weights. Blending matrix results is inexpensive but not generally a rigid transformation, so twisting joints can lose volume. Pose blending happens earlier and is a different operation.

equation.expression: x′ᵢ = Σ_j wᵢj (G_j B_j⁻¹) xᵢ,   Σ_j wᵢj=1
note: xᵢ and x′ᵢ are the bind-pose and deformed vertex positions; wᵢj are normalized skin weights.
G_j is the current global bone transform and B_j⁻¹ removes its bind-pose transform.

details.explanation: DQS encodes each bind-relative rigid skinning transform as a dual quaternion, aligns equivalent signs, blends by skin weights, and normalizes before transforming the vertex. It reduces twist collapse but can bulge and does not directly encode general nonuniform scale or shear.

equation.expression: q̂ᵢ = normalize(Σ_j wᵢj s_j q̂_j),   s_j∈{−1,+1}
note: q̂_j are unit dual quaternions and wᵢj are skin weights.
s_j aligns equivalent signs before blending; normalization produces the vertex’s rigid transform.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Authoring automation and motion transfer solve different input problems.

details.explanation: Automatic rigging infers joint placement and hierarchy; automatic skinning estimates influences, for example from heat or interior geodesic distances. Predicting a skeleton does not by itself determine usable weights.
Maps an existing motion to a differently proportioned skeleton. Chain correspondence and aligned reference poses define the mapping; end-effector correction helps preserve contacts.

aiResearch.summary: Current learned rig research targets two different production stages. RigAnything and UniRig infer a usable skeleton hierarchy and skinning weights from geometry; STaR assumes characters are already rigged and transfers a motion sequence while reducing penetration and temporal jitter. The learned stage automates authoring or retargeting, but its outputs still obey conventional skeleton, skin-weight, and animation-curve contracts.

explanations.title: RigAnything: generate a skeleton as an ordered tree
text: The input is an arbitrary 3D asset rather than a category-specific skeleton template. RigAnything orders joints breadth-first and autoregressively predicts each joint position together with its parent index, turning a tree-generation problem into a sequence-generation problem.

A diffusion component refines joint placement, and the system also assigns skinning weights. The exported result is not a new runtime rig format; it is a conventional hierarchy and vertex-to-joint influence map that existing animation tools can consume.

explanations.title: UniRig: share one learned representation across asset categories
text: UniRig encodes skeleton hierarchy with Skeleton Tree Tokenization and predicts the tree with a large autoregressive model. It then uses bone-point cross-attention to connect the predicted bones with surface geometry and estimate skinning weights.

Its Rig-XL training set spans more than 14,000 rigged models, which supports categories beyond standard humanoids. Even so, the deliverables remain the familiar pair: a topologically valid skeleton and normalized skinning influences.

explanations.title: STaR: retarget a complete sequence instead of isolated poses
text: STaR receives source motion and differently shaped source and target characters. Its spatial module uses dense shape information and a limb-penetration constraint to preserve motion meaning while reducing limb-body and limb-limb intersections.

Its temporal transformer predicts the sequence jointly, with short- and long-range consistency constraints that reduce jitter. The output is target-skeleton motion; deterministic FK, IK, constraints, and skinning still evaluate that motion at runtime.

sections.heading: Skin deformation: correctives, helper bones, and muscle
paragraphs: Skin deformation adds pose correctives, helper transforms, or tissue simulation where basic skinning loses the intended silhouette or volume. These layers repair specific behavior rather than replacing the pose system.

Evaluation order depends on the rig: skeletal motion supplies boundary conditions, tissue models generate internal deformation, and authored corrections adjust selected regions. Contact may participate in the solve rather than only being checked at the end.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Correctives repair predictable geometric errors.

details.explanation: Activates sculpted corrective offsets from joint pose rather than time. This repairs combinations such as a raised arm and bent shoulder; the base blend-shape representation is described in the face section.

note: x_skin is the base skinned position; Δx_k is a corrective offset.
φ_k(θ) activates each corrective from the current joint pose θ.

details.explanation: Adds non-anatomical controls to support a silhouette or distribute axial rotation along a limb, reducing concentrated twisting artifacts.
Restricts unintended local shrinking or swelling. A near-unit deformation determinant is a useful local measure, but volume preservation alone does not prevent intersections.

note: F is the local deformation gradient; det(F) is the deformed-to-rest volume ratio.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Tissue models add material response beneath the visible surface.

details.explanation: Changes active stress or target fiber length, allowing contraction to shape surrounding tissue. This is a control input to a muscle model, not a synonym for a blend-shape weight.

Finite elements discretize muscle, fat, and skin into material regions. Internal forces, inertia, damping, and contact determine the motion; sliding interfaces allow layers to move relative to one another.

equation.expression: M ẍ + C ẋ + f_int(x,a) = f_ext
note: x collects tissue-node positions; M and C are mass and damping matrices.
f_int depends on deformation and muscle activation a; f_ext collects external forces.
The acceleration and velocity terms give dynamics; omitting them yields a static equilibrium problem.

aiResearch.summary: These three studies address different stages: Neural Deformation Gradients reconstructs posed tissue volumes, PhysSkin learns a compact space for physical simulation, and cut-cell skinning improves the geometric input to neural weight prediction. They complement skin deformation without constituting one complete muscle-and-contact system.

explanations.title: Neural Deformation Gradients: reconstruct tissue from local deformation
text: The 2026 study takes body-shape parameters and joint rotations. Training examples come from quasi-static finite-element simulations of layered muscle and fat. The network predicts residual deformation gradients, describing local stretch, shear, and rotation, instead of directly predicting vertex offsets.

A Poisson solve reconstructs consistent vertex positions from the gradients while constraining the bone boundary; embedded meshes recover detailed anatomy. This improves volume preservation and resistance to element inversion. It approximates posed equilibrium shapes, so it does not itself model inertial tissue wobble.

explanations.title: PhysSkin: learn a deformation space, then simulate motion
text: PhysSkin (CVPR 2026) learns continuous skinning fields from static geometry without annotated weights or simulation trajectories. A shape encoder and cross-attention decoder predict how spatial points respond to a small set of deformation handles.

Self-supervision balances elastic energy, spatial smoothness, and orthogonality. During animation, a reduced physical solver updates the handle transformations, and the learned fields reconstruct full geometry. Its handles are simulation coordinates; they need not correspond to anatomical bones.

explanations.title: Cut-cell skinning: guide weight prediction with interior distances
text: A Geodesic Cut-Cell Prior for Neural Skinning (August 2026 preprint) starts from a mesh and skeleton. It combines surface connections with grid segments inside the object, creating a graph that approximates distances through the volume. Distance kernels convert these distances into a geometric skinning prior.

Neural skinning models use this prior to improve weight prediction. The graph construction is a geometric algorithm; learning occurs in the model that consumes it. This improves binding, but does not directly simulate muscle contraction, tissue sliding, or contact.

sections.heading: Hair simulation: rods, guides, and collisions
paragraphs: Hair is usually modeled as slender elastic strands attached to a moving scalp. Stretch, bend, twist, and damping belong to the material model; gravity and wind supply loads, while contact couples hair to the body and neighboring strands.
Production systems often simulate sparse guides and reconstruct dense hair. The important choices are the rod model, how guide motion is transferred, and how contact survives that reconstruction.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Representation determines the strand motion a solver can express.

details.explanation: Simulates representative strands and reconstructs neighboring fibers using their motion and local offsets. Safe guide motion does not guarantee collision-free interpolation for the followers.
Uses a sampled centerline and material frames to discretize bending and twisting geometrically. This carries rotational information that a simple position-only spring chain lacks.

Treats centerline position and cross-section orientation as independent fields, supporting stretch, shear, bend, and twist. Discretization and constraints determine which modes the implementation retains.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Contact couples strands to the body and to one another.

details.explanation: Contact prevents penetration against the body and other strands; tangential friction governs sliding and contributes to clump behavior. Dense interactions often dominate simulation cost.

aiResearch.summary: Quaffure predicts pose-dependent equilibrium drapes, HairFormer adds history-dependent dynamics, and SimAvatar generates separate hair geometry for existing simulators. The first two learn hair deformation; the third connects asset generation, physical animation, and appearance.

explanations.title: Quaffure: predict how hair settles around a pose
text: Quaffure (CVPR 2025) takes a hairstyle, body shape, and pose. An autoencoder compresses scalp-indexed strand geometry into a hairstyle code. A transformation first attaches the hair to the posed scalp, then a convolutional decoder predicts per-vertex displacements from the code and body parameters.

Training uses elastic, gravity, body-collision, and hair-density losses without precomputed simulation trajectories. At inference, adding the predicted displacements produces a quasi-static drape. This predicts the settled shape for a pose; it does not reproduce inertial swing after a sudden head movement.

explanations.title: HairFormer: combine static draping with motion history
text: HairFormer (July 2025 preprint) starts from a hairstyle code, body shape, and pose sequence. A static attention network predicts a drape; a recurrent motion encoder then captures recent pose changes and accelerations. Cross-attention combines that motion information with static hair features to predict dynamic deformation.

Physics-based self-supervision includes shape, contact, and inertia terms. The output retains strand geometry while adding delayed motion and secondary oscillation. Abrupt, difficult motions may require sequence-specific fine-tuning; the model also omits explicit strand twist, so it does not reproduce every rod degree of freedom.

explanations.title: SimAvatar: generate separate hair that can be simulated
text: SimAvatar (CVPR 2025) takes a text description and generates body, garment, and strand-based hair geometry as separate layers. It attaches 3D Gaussians to these layers and optimizes appearance using image-diffusion guidance, keeping the geometry suitable for simulation.

Given a pose sequence, existing simulators animate the hair strands and garments; their motion is transferred to the attached Gaussians for rendering. The learned contribution is asset generation and appearance. Hair dynamics still depends on the simulator rather than a network directly predicting the next hair state.

equations.label: Strand elastic energy
equations.expression: E = ½∫(k_s ε² + k_b|κ-κ₀|² + k_t(τ-τ₀)²) ds
terms: ε measures stretch; κ-κ₀ and τ-τ₀ measure departures from rest curvature and twist.
k_s, k_b, and k_t weight the three deformation modes; integration runs along the strand.

sections.heading: Face animation: semantic controls and blend shapes
paragraphs: Facial animation needs an editable representation of expression as well as speech timing and gaze. Blend shapes handle detailed surface offsets, while jaw and eye controls provide articulated motion.
Neutral geometry and shape weights define the basic face model below. Pose-dependent combination repairs use the corrective layer described in Skin deformation.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Expression representations separate controls from the character’s geometry.

details.explanation: FACS describes observable facial actions using action units, such as an inner-brow raise. It is a descriptive coding system, not a mesh representation or an emotion classifier.

A blend-shape target stores offsets from neutral geometry; its weight controls contribution to the final face. Interchange morph targets can also carry normal and tangent deltas. These are related asset and runtime views of the same mechanism.
A learned parametric head model separating identity, expression, and pose, with articulated jaw and neck controls. Its shared topology provides a consistent fitting and animation space across people.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Capture and audio models provide different evidence for driving the face.

details.explanation: Estimates facial motion from an actor’s recorded performance, then fits the target rig’s expression controls. Different proportions require an expression mapping rather than direct reuse of vertex positions.
Predicts mouth timing and coarticulation from speech; upper-face expression also depends on learned priors or explicit controls. Audio does not uniquely determine a complete facial performance.

aiResearch.summary: OmniFaceRig builds editable facial rigs from static meshes, GaussianSpeech learns personalized talking-head appearance and motion, and Audio2Face-3D converts speech into facial animation that can be retargeted. Their outputs differ: rig assets, rendered avatars, and animation data.

explanations.title: OmniFaceRig: build a rig and mouth interior from a static mesh
text: OmniFaceRig (June 2026 preprint) takes a character surface without a modeled oral cavity. Vision-language and computer-vision components screen inputs and locate the face; dense keypoints register a suitable facial template to the mesh.

Procedural fitting adds teeth, gums, and tongue, while collision-aware transfer creates facial blend shapes. The output is an editable rig with mouth geometry and repacked textures. Learned perception works alongside registration and procedural modeling; a separate animation source must still drive the rig.

explanations.title: GaussianSpeech: drive a personalized Gaussian head with speech
text: GaussianSpeech (ICCV 2025) first fits a person-specific avatar to synchronized multi-view video and audio. It tracks a FLAME face, attaches 3D Gaussians to its triangles, and learns expression-dependent appearance with wrinkle and perceptual losses.

At inference, speech features drive lip, expression, and motion prediction, which animates the personalized Gaussian representation for rendering. This models both movement and fine appearance; creating another identity requires its own avatar fitting rather than merely transferring existing blend-shape weights.

explanations.title: Audio2Face-3D: predict facial geometry, then solve rig weights
text: The 2025 Audio2Face-3D paper describes regression and diffusion variants. Speech and emotion controls condition facial motion: the regression model predicts individual poses, while the diffusion model generates short animation sequences and supports multiple identities.

The main pipeline predicts facial geometry, then fits blend-shape weights to reproduce it. Equivalent shapes on a target character enable retargeting. Geometry prediction and rig fitting are separate stages, and the target rig must provide a compatible expression vocabulary.

sections.heading: Playback: tracks, montages, layers, and root motion
paragraphs: Playback converts a clip time into a pose. It resolves the interval between stored keys, samples each track, and processes loops and playback rate. Montage routing, body masks, additive offsets, and root-motion extraction then determine how that pose contributes to the character.

An animation track is a time-varying channel; an animation pose is the collection of sampled joint transforms and other values. Keep their reference poses and coordinate spaces consistent before combining them.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Sampling chooses values in time; a Montage organizes playback and graph routing.

details.explanation: For t between key times t₀ and t₁, compute α = (t−t₀)/(t₁−t₀). Translation and scale may use linear or cubic interpolation; rotations need a rotation-aware rule. The neighboring keys belong to the clip, not necessarily adjacent rendered frames. Handle end points and looping explicitly.

note: Assume t₀ < t₁ and clamp or wrap clip time according to playback policy.

details.explanation: Sections define named time ranges and links for jumping or looping. Slot tracks contain animation segments; matching Slot nodes route their evaluated poses into the animation graph. Blend-in/out weights and body layers still affect the result, so a Montage is more than selecting one clip by time.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Layering combines body regions or reference-relative changes; root motion moves the actor.

details.explanation: Masks can blend upper-body aiming over locomotion. Additive animation stores a change relative to a base pose and applies a weighted change to the current pose. Translation uses subtraction/addition, while rotations use relative quaternion composition; scale follows the codec’s delta or ratio convention. Local-space and mesh-space additives are not interchangeable.

equation.expression: Δp = p_anim − p_base;   p_out = p_current + w Δp
note: This equation covers translation only; quaternion rotation is composed rather than added component-wise.

details.explanation: Extract the root transform change over the evaluated interval, convert it into the movement system’s space, and let that system apply actor displacement with collision and movement-mode rules. Avoid applying the same displacement again in the skeleton. Motion warping modifies an extraction window so an authored movement reaches a scene target.

sections.heading: Blending: parameter weights and transition continuity
paragraphs: A blend tree composes pose-producing nodes. Parameters choose weights, per-bone operations combine transforms, and transition methods connect changing sources. These are separate from skin weights, which combine bone influences on a vertex.
A walk-to-run blend also needs compatible gait phase. A smoother weight curve alone does not guarantee planted feet or correct scene contact; synchronization and IK can supply those constraints.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Blend spaces choose sample weights; pose blending evaluates each bone.

details.explanation: Blend corresponding bone translations and scales with weights, while normalizing or spherically interpolating rotations with sign alignment. Use compatible skeletons and spaces. Blending full matrix entries indiscriminately can introduce unintended scale or shear.

Find the two samples bracketing a scalar input such as speed. The normalized interval position determines their weights. Outside the sample range, define clamping or another explicit boundary rule; coincident sample coordinates need special handling.

note: Assume s₀ < s₁ and s is inside the interval.

details.explanation: A two-parameter space can triangulate sample positions, locate the containing triangle, and use its barycentric coordinates as three animation weights. Nondegenerate interior weights sum to one and are nonnegative. Other 2D schemes exist; handle outside-hull queries and degenerate layouts explicitly.

equation.expression: p = w₀a + w₁b + w₂c;   w₀ + w₁ + w₂ = 1
note: p, a, b, c are points in parameter space, not mesh vertices undergoing skinning.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Crossfade evaluates two moving sources; inertialization decays a captured residual.

details.explanation: During a transition, continue evaluating old and new animations and vary their blend weights over time. It preserves both source evolutions but costs two evaluations and may mix incompatible contacts. State transitions can request this blend without defining the interpolation rule themselves.

At a switch, capture pose and velocity offsets between the displayed state and the new source. Continue evaluating the new animation and decay the stored residual with a continuity-aware function. Rotations need relative orientation offsets. An inertial transition requests this mechanism; the old source need not keep running.

sections.heading: Interpolation: vectors, rotations, curves, and springs
paragraphs: Interpolation computes values between samples; its path and timing are separate choices. A curve parameter moving at constant speed does not necessarily produce constant spatial speed. Quaternion interpolation also needs consistent signs because q and −q represent the same rotation.

Lerp, Nlerp, and Slerp combine endpoints. Hermite, Bézier, and Catmull–Rom describe curve shape using tangents or nearby controls. Spring interpolation is different: it advances a state with velocity toward a target, so previous motion influences the next result.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Choose interpolation according to the value’s geometry.

details.explanation: Use (1−α)a + αb for scalars or vectors. For α between zero and one, the result lies on the straight segment. Consecutive linear segments are position-continuous but their velocities can jump at keys. A raw quaternion lerp is not generally unit length.

Align quaternion signs, linearly interpolate, then normalize. It is inexpensive and follows the short rotation arc under that sign convention, but generally not at constant angular speed. Opposite quaternion signs must be resolved before interpolating to avoid a zero-length midpoint.

note: Use s = −1 when q₀·q₁ < 0, otherwise s = +1.

details.explanation: Interpolate unit quaternions along a great-circle arc on the four-dimensional unit sphere. With aligned signs and a linear time parameter, the physical rotation follows the short arc at constant angular speed. Nearly identical endpoints need a stable small-angle fallback such as Nlerp.

note: Ω is the unit-quaternion angle after sign alignment; endpoints are normalized.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Cubic curves differ in how their controls specify endpoints and tangents.

details.explanation: A cubic Hermite segment uses two endpoint values and two endpoint tangents. Tangents are derivatives with respect to a parameter: if stored per second but evaluated on a normalized interval, scale them by the interval duration. Consistent joining derivatives provide velocity continuity.

equation.expression: p(u) = h₀₀(u)p₀ + h₁₀(u)Δt v₀ + h₀₁(u)p₁ + h₁₁(u)Δt v₁
note: h terms are cubic Hermite basis functions; u is normalized time and v₀,v₁ are endpoint derivatives per second.

details.explanation: A cubic Bézier curve uses four control points: it passes through the first and last, while the inner points control endpoint tangents. Evaluate with Bernstein polynomials or repeated interpolation through de Casteljau’s algorithm. An easing curve mapping time to progress may require solving its horizontal coordinate first.

Four neighboring controls define the segment through the middle two; the outer controls determine tangents. Uniform, chordal, and centripetal parameterizations produce different shapes when points are unevenly spaced. Passing through keys alone does not ensure constant speed or prevent all overshoot.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Spring interpolation evolves a state instead of selecting a fixed point between endpoints.

details.explanation: Use displacement from a target and current velocity in a damped spring model. Stiffness controls response speed and damping controls oscillation; the target may move every frame. Integrate stably or use an analytic update for a fixed target over the step. Rotations require an orientation-error representation rather than raw quaternion component springs.

equation.expression: m ẍ + c ẋ + k(x − x_target) = 0
note: This form uses a target treated as fixed during the step; m, c, k are mass, damping, and stiffness.

sections.heading: State machines: discrete decisions around continuous motion
paragraphs: A state machine chooses which motion-producing branch is active; a blend space varies motion continuously inside that branch. For example, Grounded can contain Idle and Locomotion, while Airborne contains Jump and Fall.

Evaluate transition conditions from a consistent update snapshot, apply priority and interruption rules, then request a crossfade or inertial transition. The transition trigger and pose-smoothing method should remain separate concepts.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: State hierarchy organizes decisions; rules decide when a transition is allowed.

details.explanation: Maintain an active state and test its eligible outgoing transitions on updates. If a rule succeeds, choose a destination according to configured priorities and interruption behavior. The state can contain a clip player or an entire blend graph; a transition may temporarily evaluate both states.

A parent state contains a child machine, forming an active path through the hierarchy. Parent-level transitions can leave a whole subtree, while child transitions refine local behavior. Entry, exit, history, and transition priority depend on the engine and configuration; a hierarchy is not a set of unrelated machines.

Compute whether a transition is allowed from inputs such as speed, grounded state, or remaining animation time. Threshold hysteresis prevents rapid toggling: entry and exit need not share the same speed threshold. A true rule permits the transition; its blend duration and smoothing are separate settings.

sections.heading: Compression and trimming: spend bits where motion needs them
paragraphs: Trimming changes the intended clip; compression approximates the retained clip within an error budget. Fewer keys, fewer bits, compact rotation representations, and fitted curves reduce different parts of storage and have different decoding costs.

A small local rotation error near the root can move a hand substantially. Measure reconstructed motion in meaningful spaces and include end effectors, skin deformation, additive use, and root-motion continuity when selecting tolerances.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Distinguish intentional edits from error-bounded temporal simplification.

details.explanation: Keep an intended time interval and update its local time origin, looping policy, and dependent events. Root-motion deltas, synchronization markers, and additive references need to remain consistent with the new boundaries. Removing unused content is an authoring decision rather than lossy reconstruction.

Test whether removing a key lets neighboring retained keys reconstruct the original motion within a tolerance. Evaluate interpolation error between keys, not only at retained samples, and protect important discontinuities or event timing. Constant and default tracks may be represented by one value or omitted under an explicit default rule.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Quantization reduces value precision; fitting changes the time representation.

details.explanation: Map values in a known range to b-bit integers, then reconstruct approximate floating-point values during decoding. Per-track or per-segment ranges can improve precision, at the cost of metadata. Constant ranges require a special representation; clipping outside the range creates extra error.

note: Δ is the step of uniform scalar quantization; this assumes a nonconstant range.

details.explanation: A unit quaternion has only three independent continuous components. One scheme makes the largest component positive, stores its index and the other three, then reconstructs the missing value from unit length. Fixed-component schemes such as drop-W also exist. Quantization, sign continuity, and renormalization still matter.

Approximate many samples with fewer piecewise-curve coefficients or controls. Choose segment count and tangents from a reconstruction tolerance. Runtime evaluates the fitted curve, whose representation need not match the original DCC spline. This differs from merely reducing bits per sample.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: A codec combines representations and error metrics rather than assigning precision blindly.

details.explanation: ACL emphasizes fast random-access decompression of uniformly sampled transform tracks, with range reduction, constant/default handling, and variable bit rates. Optional database or frame-stripping features remove less important samples under their own rules. Per-track precision or rounding does not mean arbitrary independent sampling rates for every bone.

Allocate precision according to how a joint affects the reconstructed character, not merely its local curve amplitude. End-effector, object-space, or virtual-shell distances can expose amplified rotation error. Hands, feet, and contact-critical joints may need tighter budgets; additive clips should also be assessed in their intended composition.

sections.heading: Data-driven motion: retrieval, prediction, generation, and control
paragraphs: Data-driven motion is broader than machine learning. Motion Matching searches recorded motion; neural sequence models predict or generate poses; reinforcement learning trains actions that a physics simulator executes. Their outputs enter different places in a runtime animation system.

These categories overlap. A Transformer can serve as a VAE decoder or a diffusion denoiser, and a VAE latent space can be controlled by an RL policy. Specify the input, learned objective, runtime output, and whether contact is enforced by geometry or a physical simulator.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Retrieval selects a recorded continuation using pose and trajectory features.

details.explanation: Build a query from the current pose, velocities, and desired trajectory, then search a feature-indexed database for a low-cost matching frame. Continue from that location and blend if a jump is selected. Cost weights, normalization, and continuation bias affect stability. Conventional Motion Matching needs no neural network.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Sequence models use history to predict motion; architecture does not determine the output task.

details.explanation: A recurrent network updates a hidden state from the current input and previous hidden state, then predicts a pose or pose increment. LSTM adds gated memory for longer dependencies. Train on reference sequences; runtime may feed predictions back recursively, which can accumulate drift. The carried state summarizes more than just the previous raw frame.

Encode frames, joints, or motion patches as tokens with time and spatial information, then use attention to combine context. A predictive model uses appropriate causal masking; a completion model may attend to known frames on both sides. Decode a future pose or whole sequence. Attention alone does not impose joint limits or ground contact.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: Generative motion models learn distributions, with different latent and sampling procedures.

details.explanation: Training corrupts motion at different noise levels and learns to recover noise, clean motion, or another parameterization. At runtime, denoise a noisy sequence under text, action, or keyframe conditions over multiple steps. MDM predicts clean samples rather than noise. The output is motion data; physical feasibility and sampling latency are separate concerns.

The encoder infers a latent distribution from motion and optional conditions; a sampled latent and conditions drive a decoder that reconstructs or generates motion. Reconstruction and prior regularization structure the latent space. Autoregressive conditional VAEs can generate one update at a time, so not every Motion VAE encodes a whole clip into one vector.

keywordSourceGroups.summary: A learned policy outputs controls; the simulator determines the resulting motion.

details.explanation: A policy reads simulated state and a task or reference-motion condition, then outputs torques, target joint angles, or other controls. The environment steps physics and produces reward signals. Training updates the policy from collected experience; deployment typically runs a fixed policy without learning every frame. DeepMimic combines task and imitation objectives.

aiResearch.summary: MotionCraft generates whole-body motion from multiple input modalities; MoMADiff uses text and sparse keyframes to control sequence generation; Policy-Space Diffusion generates controller parameters for physical simulation. These approaches supply motion data or control policies, while coordinate conventions and skeletal transforms remain necessary for playback.

explanations.title: MotionCraft: condition whole-body generation on text and audio
text: MotionCraft (AAAI 2025) uses a unified diffusion transformer for motion conditioned on text, speech, or music. Training first learns text-to-motion semantics, then adapts low-level multimodal controls. MC-Attn models static and dynamic body-topology graphs in parallel.

The model generates whole-body motion in the SMPL-X representation. Using that result on a production character requires mapping its pose representation to the target skeleton and evaluating its transforms. Motion generation alone does not establish physical contact or gameplay constraints.

explanations.title: MoMADiff: complete motion around specified keyframes
text: MoMADiff (ACM Multimedia 2025) encodes each motion frame into a continuous latent representation. A masked autoregressive model with a diffusion prediction head conditions generation on text and known frames. It can first generate keyframes or accept sparse user-provided ones.

The model progressively fills the missing frames and decodes a complete motion sequence. It supports learned in-betweening and keyframe control rather than multi-object interaction. The output is motion data; it does not replace skeletal transforms or constitute a physical controller.

explanations.title: Policy-Space Diffusion: generate a controller instead of a pose clip
text: This 2025 study first trains compact motion-imitation policies, using Common Neighbor Policy regularization to keep policies for nearby tasks similar in parameter space. A conditional diffusion model then learns the distribution of policy weights and biases, including variation in character morphology.

Sampling produces a new policy network. During playback, that policy responds to the simulated character state and supplies controls to a physics engine, which advances the motion. This differs from interpolating pose curves: the generated artifact is a feedback controller, whose behavior depends on the simulated character and conditions.

closing: Geometry defines the deformation domain; playback and blending produce a pose; state logic chooses transitions; skeletal evaluation and skinning move the surface. Compression must preserve reconstructed motion within an error budget. Retrieval, learned pose generation, and physical control can be combined, provided their timing, coordinate, reference-pose, and contact conventions agree.
